stem: A client says a hearing aid has stopped working. Which initial nursing check is appropriate before arranging further device evaluation?

options.A: Check that the hearing aid is powered and that the battery is not depleted, and inspect the device for visible earwax or debris
options.B: Increase the volume to the maximum setting before checking the device
options.C: Assume the client's hearing loss has suddenly worsened and discard the hearing aid
options.D: Avoid any basic check because every hearing-aid problem requires immediate device replacement

rationale: NIDCD hearing-aid guidance recommends learning how to replace batteries and clean the device and notes that earwax can clog or damage hearing aids. These are appropriate basic checks when a device is not functioning. Therefore A is the best answer. Maximum volume can be uncomfortable or unsafe, sudden worsening should not be assumed from device failure alone, and simple battery or debris problems do not automatically require replacement. Persistent malfunction or new hearing symptoms warrant appropriate professional evaluation.
educational_objective: Perform basic hearing-aid troubleshooting by checking power/battery status and visible debris while referring persistent malfunction or new hearing symptoms for appropriate evaluation.
source_organization: National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders (NIDCD), National Institutes of Health
source_locator: Sections 'How can I adjust to my hearing aid?' and 'How can I care for my hearing aid?': practice replacing batteries; earwax/fluid may clog a hearing aid; clean as instructed; replace dead batteries immediately
source_claim_supported: Basic hearing-aid care includes checking/replacing batteries and cleaning the device; earwax can interfere with hearing-aid function.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Appendix A, Basic Care and Comfort > Assistive Devices, printed p.36 / PDF p.40: assess use of assistive devices and evaluate correct use of assistive devices by the client
blueprint_topic: Basic Care and Comfort — Assistive Devices / hearing aid care
correction_summary: Changed the source item's broad 'check for earwax blockage in the device or ear canal' into a safer initial-device assessment: verify power/battery status and inspect the hearing aid itself for visible wax/debris. Added explicit escalation for persistent malfunction or new hearing symptoms and rebuilt distractors to avoid trivial color/repair-only choices.
audit_findings: A is supported by NIDCD device-care guidance and stays within basic nursing troubleshooting. B risks inappropriate amplification; C incorrectly infers a new clinical diagnosis from device failure; D overstates the need for replacement. The answer does not authorize invasive cerumen removal or delay evaluation of sudden hearing loss. No second answer, cueing, or unresolved conflict remains.
